'''''Acacia cultriformis''''', known as '''knife-leaf wattle''', '''dogtooth wattle''', '''half-moon wattle''' or '''golden-glow wattle''',<ref name="floransw">{{cite web |last1=Kodela |first1=Phillip G. |title=''Acacia cultriformis'' |url=https://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/NSWfl.pl?page=nswfl&lvl=sp&name=Acacia~cultriformis |publisher=Royal Botanic Garden, Sydney |access-date=8 August 2025}}</ref> is a species of flowering plant in the family [[Fabaceae]] and is [[endemic]] to eastern Australia. It is widely cultivated, and has been found to have naturalised in Asia, Africa, North America, New Zealand and South America.<ref name="PoWO">{{cite web |title=''Acacia cultriformis'' |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:470087-1#synonyms |publisher=Plants of the World Online |access-date=8 August 2025}}</ref> ''A. cultriformis'' grows to a height of about 4 m (13 ft) and has triangle-shaped [[phyllode]]s. The yellow flowers appear from August to November in its natural range. Its attractive foliage and bright flowers make it a popular garden plant.

==Description==
[[File:Acacia cultriformis Montjuic.jpg|thumb|Triangle-shaped leaves]]
[[File:Acacia cultriformis habit.jpg|thumb|Habit in the [[Australian Botanic Garden Mount Annan|Mount Annan Botanic Gardens]]]]
''Acacia cultriformis'' is a woody shrub with an upright or spreading [[Habit (biology)|habit]] that grows up to {{cvt|4|m}} high. Its branchlets may be bare and smooth or [[pruinescence|covered with a white bloom]].<ref name=floransw/> The phyllodes are rather crowded, leathery, green-grey and asymmetrical, {{cvt|10–30|mm}} long and {{cvt|5–15|mm}} wide, with one leaf margin angled so the overall shape is triangular. There is a rather prominent [[Gland (botany)|gland]] at the widest part of the phyllode.<ref name=floransw/><ref name="FoA">{{cite web |last1=Maslin |first1=Bruce R. |last2=Kodela |first2=Phillip G. |title=''Acacia cultriformis'' |url=https://profiles.ala.org.au/opus/foa/profile/Acacia%20cultriformis |publisher=Flora of Australia. Australian Biological Resources Study, Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water: Canberra. |access-date=9 August 2025}}</ref><ref name="lucid">{{cite web |title=''Acacia cultriformis'' |url=https://apps.lucidcentral.org/wattle/text/entities/acacia_cultriformis.htm |publisher=Australian Biological Resources Study |access-date=9 August 2025}}</ref><ref name="www">{{cite web |title=''Acacia cultriformis'' |url=https://worldwidewattle.com/speciesgallery/cultriformis.php |publisher=World Wide Wattle |access-date=9 August 2025}}</ref> Flowering takes place from August to November, 

The flowers are borne in spherical or  shortly cylindrical heads in [[raceme]]s {{cvt|10–50|mm}} long, (sometimes up to {{cvt|200|mm}} long) in axils, on [[Peduncle (botany)|peduncles]] {{cvt|2.5–5|mm}} long. Each head contains 13 to 40 bright golden yellow flowers. Flowering occurs from August to November<ref name=floransw/> and can be prolific on upper parts of the plant.<ref name="FoA"/> The pods are narrowly oblong,<ref name="FoA" /> straight or slightly curved, more or less flat raised over the seeds, up to {{cvt|90|mm}} long and {{cvt|5–8|mm}} wide and firmly papery to thinly leathery.<ref name="floransw" /><ref name="FoA" /> The seeds are {{cvt|3.5–4.5|mm}} long, black and dull to slightly shiny, with a club-shaped [[aril]].<ref name="FoA"/>

The related ''[[Acacia semilunata]]'' is similar in appearance but has hairy branchlets and narrower seed pods.<ref name="FoA"/> ''[[Acacia pravissima]]'' can look similar but has a secondary longitudinal vein in its phyllodes.<ref name="FoA"/>

==Taxonomy==
''Acacia cultriformis'' was first formally described in 1832 by Scottish botanist [[George Don]] in his book, ''A General History of Dichlamydeous Plants'', and Don gave it the common name 'cultriform-leaved acacia'.<ref name=APNI>{{cite web|title=''Acacia cultriformis'' |url=https://biodiversity.org.au/nsl/services/rest/instance/apni/466374 |publisher=APNI|access-date=9 August 2025}}</ref><ref name="G.Don">{{cite book |last1=Don |first1=George |title=A General History of Dichlamydeous Plants |volume=2 |date=1832 |location=London |page=406 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/62428#page/420/mode/1up |access-date=9 August 2025}}</ref> The [[specific epithet]] (''cultriformis'') means 'curved like a short wide [[scimitar]]'.<ref name="Stearn">{{cite book |last1=Stearn |first1=William T. |title=Botanical Latin |date=1992 |publisher=Timber Press |location=Portland, Oregon |page=395 |edition=fourth}}</ref>

Queensland botanist [[Leslie Pedley|Les Pedley]] reclassified the species as ''Racosperma cultriforme'' in 2003, in his proposal to reclassify almost all Australian members of the genus into the new genus ''[[Racosperma]]''.<ref name="pedley">{{cite journal |last1=Pedley |first1=Leslie |title=A synopsis of Racosperma C. Mart. (Leguminosae: Mimosoideae) |journal=Austrobaileya: A Journal of Plant Systematics |date=2003 |volume=6 |issue=3 |pages=445–496 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/281479#page/101/mode/1up |access-date=9 August 2025}}</ref> This name is treated as a [[Synonym (taxonomy)|synonym]] of ''Acacia cultriformis'' by the [[Australian Plant Census]].<ref name="APC" />

==Distribution and habitat==
''Acacia cultriformis'' is found on the western slopes of the [[Great Dividing Range]] in central [[New South Wales]] and southern [[Queensland]]. It occurs discontinuously north from [[Wagga Wagga]] and [[Narrandera]] to west of the [[Denman, New South Wales |Denman]] - [[Singleton, New South Wales|Singleton]] area,<ref name=floransw/> and to [[Stanthorpe]] and [[Inglewood, Queensland|Inglewood]] in south-eastern Queensland.<ref name="FoA" /> It grows in clay-loam or sandstone soils in ''Eucalyptus'' woodland,<ref name="FoA" /> often on rocky ridges.<ref name=EJ>{{cite book | last1=Elliot | first1=Rodger W. | last2=Jones | first2=David L. | last3=Blake | first3=Trevor |title=Encyclopaedia of Australian Plants Suitable for Cultivation: Vol. 2|year=1985|publisher=Lothian Press |location=Port Melbourne, Victoria |isbn=978-0-85091-143-5|page=37 }}</ref>

== Uses and cultivation==
Its bright flowers and attractive leaves make ''Acacia cultriformis'' one of the most popular wattles in cultivation. Adaptable to the garden, it is grown in a wide range of soils and can tolerate frosts. It grows in sun or part shade.<ref name="anpsa">{{cite web|url=http://anpsa.org.au/a-cul.html|title=''Acacia cultriformis'' |last=Walters|first=Brian|date=February 2012|work=Plant Guides|publisher=Australian Native Plants Society (Australia)|access-date=20 September 2014|archive-date=22 February 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150222071028/http://anpsa.org.au/a-cul.html|url-status=dead}}</ref> Drought tolerant, it can be used to combat soil erosion.<ref name=EJ/> ''Acacia'' 'Cascade' (RN: ACC154) is a prostrate form that spreads to a diameter of 2 m (7 ft). It was registered on 18 November 1982, having been propagated by [[Bill Molyneux]] at his nursery in [[Montrose, Victoria]] from a selected seedling.<ref name=ib29>{{cite web
  | last = [[Australian Cultivar Registration Authority]]
  | title = Acacia 'Cascade'
  | work = Descriptions of Registered Cultivars  
  | publisher = Australian National Botanic Gardens
  | year = 2009
  | url = http://www.anbg.gov.au/acra/descriptions/acc154.html
  | access-date = 19 September 2014}}</ref> It makes an attractive cascading plant in a [[rockery]].<ref name="anpsa"/>

''A. cultriformis'' is used as [[cut flowers]].<ref>[http://asgap.org.au/APOL4/dec96-2.html Australian Plants as Cut Flowers] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070818191650/http://asgap.org.au/APOL4/dec96-2.html |date=18 August 2007 }}</ref>
The flowers are edible and they are an ingredient used in some [[fritter]]s.<ref>{{cite web|title=Knife-Leaf Wattle (''Acacia cultriformis'')|access-date=11 October 2019|website=garden.org|url=https://garden.org/plants/view/119018/Knife-Leaf-Wattle-Acacia-cultriformis/}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Acacia Flower Fritters Recipe|author=Danièle Mazet-Delpeuch|website=thedailymeal.com|date=12 September 2013 |access-date=11 October 2019|url=https://www.thedailymeal.com/acacia-flower-fritters-recipe}}</ref> Yellow [[dye]] is extracted from the flowers and green dye is extracted from the seed pods.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.pfaf.org/database/plants.php?Acacia+cultriformis |title=''Acacia cultriformis'' – Plants for a Future database report |publisher=pfaf.org|access-date=2008-05-18}}
</ref>
